claim: Recursive procedures that allow placing a vocal signal inside another of a similar kind provide a neuro-computational blueprint for syntax and phonology in spoken language and human song.
source: Recursive procedures that allow placing a vocal signal inside another of a similar kind provide a neuro-computational blueprint for syntax and phonology in spoken language and human song.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical role of recursion in language and music, drawing from established scientific understanding in linguistics and cognitive science.

claim: There are no known vocal sequences among nonhuman primates arranged in self-embedded patterns that evince vocal recursion or potential incipient or evolutionary transitional forms thereof.
source: There are, however, no known vocal sequences among nonhuman primates arranged in self-embedded patterns that evince vocal recursion or potential incipient or evolutionary transitional forms thereof, suggesting a neuro-cognitive transformation exclusive to humans.
evidence: This claim reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study, based on the absence of documented cases in the literature.

claim: Wild flanged male orangutan long calls feature rhythmically isochronous call sequences nested within isochronous call sequences, consistent with two hierarchical strata.
source: Here, we uncover that wild flanged male orangutan long calls feature rhythmically isochronous call sequences nested within isochronous call sequences, consistent with two hierarchical strata.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by rhythmic analyses of 66 long call recordings from 10 orangutans.

claim: Three temporally and acoustically distinct call rhythms in the lower stratum were not related to the overarching rhythm at the higher stratum by any low multiples.
source: Remarkably, three temporally and acoustically distinct call rhythms in the lower stratum were not related to the overarching rhythm at the higher stratum by any low multiples, which suggests that these recursive structures were neither the result of parallel non-hierarchical procedures nor anatomical artifacts of bodily constraints or resonances.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis showing the ratio of sub-pulses to full pulses is approximately 1:22, not a small integer multiple.

claim: The recursive structures in orangutan long calls were neither the result of parallel non-hierarchical procedures nor anatomical artifacts of bodily constraints or resonances.
source: Remarkably, three temporally and acoustically distinct call rhythms in the lower stratum were not related to the overarching rhythm at the higher stratum by any low multiples, which suggests that these recursive structures were neither the result of parallel non-hierarchical procedures nor anatomical artifacts of bodily constraints or resonances.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the rhythmic ratios are not small integer multiples, which would be expected from physiological constraints.

claim: Second-order combinatorics involving hierarchically organized and cyclically structured vocal sounds in ancient hominids may have preluded the evolution of recursion in modern language-able humans.
source: Second-order combinatorics, 'sequences within sequences', involving hierarchically organized and cyclically structured vocal sounds in ancient hominids may have preluded the evolution of recursion in modern language-able humans.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation of the findings.

claim: Recursion represents the repetition of an element or pattern within a self-similar element or pattern.
source: Among the many definitions of recursion (Martins, 2012), the view that it represents the repetition of an element or pattern within a self-similar element or pattern has crossed centuries and disciplines, from von Humboldt, 1836 and Hockett, 1960 to Mandelbrot, 1980 and Chomsky, 2010; from fractals in mathematics (Mandelbrot, 1980) to generative grammars in linguistics (Chomsky, 2010), from graphic (e.g., 'Print Gallery' by M. C. Escher) to popular art (e.g., 1940's Batman #8 comic book cover).
evidence: This definition is supported by citations to multiple scholarly works across different fields.

claim: Recursion is an operation that produces multiple, potentially infinite sets of items from one initial item or a finite set by nesting an item within itself or within another item of the same kind.
source: Across varying terminologies, the common denominator across fields is that to re-curse (from the Latin to 're-run' or 're-invoke') is an operation that produces multiple, potentially infinite sets of items from one initial item or a finite set. This is achieved by nesting an item within itself or within another item of the same kind.
evidence: This is a conceptual definition drawing from established understanding across multiple disciplines.

claim: Recursion is not the simple repetition of a pattern or item on a single level, but the placement of a pattern or item within itself, generating different hierarchical levels or strata.
source: Accordingly, recursion is not the simple repetition of a pattern or item on a single level (e.g., computer folders or Russian dolls side by side), but the placement of a pattern or item within itself (e.g., computer folders or Russian dolls inside each other), hence, generating different hierarchical levels or strata.
evidence: This is a conceptual clarification of what distinguishes recursion from simple repetition.

claim: In recursion, the same pattern or item is encountered at least at two different scales.
source: This means that the same pattern or item is encountered at least at two different scales (e.g., 12 at the scale of hours, and 12 at the scale of minutes).
evidence: This is a definitional characteristic of recursion, illustrated with an example.

claim: Recursion and its diagnostic self-embedded patterns have been recognized in phonology.
source: In language, although classically associated with syntax (Chomsky, 2010; Idsardi et al., 2018), recursion and its diagnostic self-embedded patterns have been recognized in phonology (Bennett, 2018; Elfner, 2015; Barış and Revithiadou, 2009; Nasukawa, 2015; Nasukawa, 2020; Vogel, 2012) and in verbal and non-verbal music (Jackendoff, 2009; Koelsch et al., 2013; Martins et al., 2017; Sharma and Chimalakonda, 2018), making these systems open-ended and theoretically inexhaustible.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to scholarly work on recursion in phonology.

claim: Recursion and its diagnostic self-embedded patterns have been recognized in verbal and non-verbal music.
source: In language, although classically associated with syntax (Chomsky, 2010; Idsardi et al., 2018), recursion and its diagnostic self-embedded patterns have been recognized in phonology (Bennett, 2018; Elfner, 2015; Barış and Revithiadou, 2009; Nasukawa, 2015; Nasukawa, 2020; Vogel, 2012) and in verbal and non-verbal music (Jackendoff, 2009; Koelsch et al., 2013; Martins et al., 2017; Sharma and Chimalakonda, 2018), making these systems open-ended and theoretically inexhaustible.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to scholarly work on recursion in music.

claim: Recursion makes language, phonology, and music systems open-ended and theoretically inexhaustible.
source: In language, although classically associated with syntax (Chomsky, 2010; Idsardi et al., 2018), recursion and its diagnostic self-embedded patterns have been recognized in phonology (Bennett, 2018; Elfner, 2015; Barış and Revithiadou, 2009; Nasukawa, 2015; Nasukawa, 2020; Vogel, 2012) and in verbal and non-verbal music (Jackendoff, 2009; Koelsch et al., 2013; Martins et al., 2017; Sharma and Chimalakonda, 2018), making these systems open-ended and theoretically inexhaustible.
evidence: This is a theoretical consequence of recursion in these systems, drawing from established linguistic and musicological theory.

claim: The apparent absence of recursive vocal sequences in nonhuman primates, notably in great apes, has been interpreted as indicating that a neuro-cognitive or neuro-computational transformation occurred in the human lineage but none other.
source: However, their apparent absence, notably in great apes – our closest living relatives – has been interpreted as indicating that a neuro-cognitive or neuro-computational transformation occurred in our lineage but none other (Hauser et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hauser et al., 2002, representing an interpretation in the literature.

claim: The absence of evidence for recursion in nonhuman primates has led some scholars to question the role of natural selection for the emergence of language, tacitly favoring sudden 'hopeful monster' mutant scenarios.
source: This absence of evidence has led some scholars to question altogether the role of natural selection for the emergence of language, tacitly favoring sudden 'hopeful monster' mutant scenarios (Berwick and Chomsky, 2019; Bolhuis and Wynne, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to scholarly works that propose non-gradualist evolutionary scenarios.

claim: Syntax-like vocal combinatorics have been identified in some bird species.
source: Syntax-like vocal combinatorics have been identified in some bird (Engesser et al., 2019; Engesser et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2017) and primate species (Jiang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2020), but vocal combinatorics were not claimed to be recursive nor was recursion directly tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on bird vocalizations.

claim: Syntax-like vocal combinatorics have been identified in some primate species.
source: Syntax-like vocal combinatorics have been identified in some bird (Engesser et al., 2019; Engesser et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2017) and primate species (Jiang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2020), but vocal combinatorics were not claimed to be recursive nor was recursion directly tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on primate vocalizations.

claim: Vocal combinatorics in birds and primates were not claimed to be recursive nor was recursion directly tested.
source: Syntax-like vocal combinatorics have been identified in some bird (Engesser et al., 2019; Engesser et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2017) and primate species (Jiang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2020), but vocal combinatorics were not claimed to be recursive nor was recursion directly tested.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of previous studies, based on review of the cited literature.

claim: European starlings can learn to recognize recursion in synthetic stimuli after dedicated human training in laboratory settings.
source: Three notable exceptions demonstrated recursion learning in nonhuman animal settings: (Gentner et al., 2006) in European starlings, Ferrigno et al., 2020 in rhesus macaques, and Liao et al., 2022 in crows. These studies show that animals can learn to recognize recursion in synthetic stimuli after dedicated human training in laboratory settings, but they do not show spontaneous production of recursive vocal combinatorics in naturalistic settings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gentner et al., 2006.

claim: Rhesus macaques can learn to recognize recursion in synthetic stimuli after dedicated human training in laboratory settings.
source: Three notable exceptions demonstrated recursion learning in nonhuman animal settings: (Gentner et al., 2006) in European starlings, Ferrigno et al., 2020 in rhesus macaques, and Liao et al., 2022 in crows. These studies show that animals can learn to recognize recursion in synthetic stimuli after dedicated human training in laboratory settings, but they do not show spontaneous production of recursive vocal combinatorics in naturalistic settings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ferrigno et al., 2020.

claim: Crows can learn to recognize recursion in synthetic stimuli after dedicated human training in laboratory settings.
source: Three notable exceptions demonstrated recursion learning in nonhuman animal settings: (Gentner et al., 2006) in European starlings, Ferrigno et al., 2020 in rhesus macaques, and Liao et al., 2022 in crows. These studies show that animals can learn to recognize recursion in synthetic stimuli after dedicated human training in laboratory settings, but they do not show spontaneous production of recursive vocal combinatorics in naturalistic settings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liao et al., 2022.

claim: Laboratory studies on recursion learning in animals do not show spontaneous production of recursive vocal combinatorics in naturalistic settings.
source: Three notable exceptions demonstrated recursion learning in nonhuman animal settings: (Gentner et al., 2006) in European starlings, Ferrigno et al., 2020 in rhesus macaques, and Liao et al., 2022 in crows. These studies show that animals can learn to recognize recursion in synthetic stimuli after dedicated human training in laboratory settings, but they do not show spontaneous production of recursive vocal combinatorics in naturalistic settings.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of the cited laboratory studies.

claim: Evidence of recursive vocal structures in wild animals, notably in primates closely related to humans, would better inform what evolutionary precursors and processes could have led to the emergence of recursion in the human lineage.
source: Evidence of recursive vocal structures in wild animals (i.e., without human priming or intervention), notably in primates closely related to humans, such as great apes, would better inform what evolutionary precursors and processes could have led to the emergence of recursion in the human lineage.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the value of studying wild animals for understanding human evolution.

claim: A structural approach to recursive vocal combinatorics requires no prior assumptions about species' cognitive capacities.
source: First, no prior assumptions are required about species' cognitive capacities. High-level neuro-motor procedures are inferred only to the extent that these are directly reflected in how signal sequences are organized.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the advantages of the structural approach used in the study.

claim: A structural approach to recursive vocal combinatorics requires no prior assumptions about signal meaning.
source: Second, no prior assumptions are required about signal meaning. There are no certain parallels between semantic content and word meaning in animals, but analyses of signal patterning allow us to identify the similarities between non-semantic (nonhuman) and semantic (human) combinatoric systems (Lipkind et al., 2013; Sainburg et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the advantages of the structural approach, supported by citations.

claim: A structural approach to recursive vocal combinatorics requires no prior assumptions about signal function.
source: Third, no prior assumptions are required about signal function. Under any evolutionary scenario, including punctuated hypotheses, ancestral signal function (whether cooperative, competitive, or otherwise) is expected to have derived or been leveraged by its proto-recursive structure.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the advantages of the structural approach.

claim: The study analyzed 66 long call audio recordings produced by 10 orangutans across approximately 2510 observation hours at Tuanan, Central Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo.
source: We conducted precise rhythm analyses (De Gregorio et al., 2021; Roeske et al., 2020) of 66 long call audio recordings produced by 10 orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus wurmbii) across approximately 2510 observation hours at Tuanan, Central Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo.
evidence: This describes the data collection for the study.

claim: Five different element types comprise the structural building blocks of long calls in wild orangutans.
source: We identified five different element types that comprise the structural building blocks of long calls in the wild (Hardus et al., 2009; Lameira and Wich, 2008), of which the primary type are full pulses (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, supported by data and references to previous work, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Full pulses are the primary element type in orangutan long calls.
source: We identified five different element types that comprise the structural building blocks of long calls in the wild (Hardus et al., 2009; Lameira and Wich, 2008), of which the primary type are full pulses (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Full pulses can break up into four different 'sub-pulse' element types: grumble sub-pulses, sub-pulse transitory elements, pulse bodies, and bubble sub-pulses.
source: Full pulses do not, however, always exhibit uninterrupted vocal production throughout a long call (as during a long call's climax; Spillmann et al., 2010) but can break up into four different 'sub-pulse' element types: (i) grumble sub-pulses (quick succession of staccato calls that typically constitute the first build-up pulses of long calls; Hardus et al., 2009), (ii) sub-pulse transitory elements and (iii) pulse bodies (typically constituting pulses before and/or after climax pulses), and (iv) bubble sub-pulses (quick succession of staccato calls that typically constitute the last tail-off pulses of long calls) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The study extracted inter-onset intervals from 8993 vocal long call elements.
source: We extracted inter-onset intervals (IOIs; i.e., time difference between the start of a vocal element and the preceding one – tk) from 8993 vocal long call elements (Figure 1A): 1930 full pulses (1916 after filtering for 0.025 < tk < 5 s), 757 grumble sub-pulses (731), 1068 sub-pulse transitory elements (374), 816 pulse bodies (11), and 4422 bubble sub-pulses (4193).
evidence: This describes the data extraction process for the study.

claim: The density probability function of orangutan full pulses showed one peak at rk = 0.493 in close vicinity to a theoretically pure isochronic rhythm.
source: The density probability function of orangutan full pulses showed one peak (rk = 0.493) in close vicinity to a theoretically pure isochronic rhythm, that is, full pulses were regularly paced at a 1:1 ratio, following a constant tempo along the long call (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's rhythm analysis, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Full pulses were regularly paced at a 1:1 ratio, following a constant tempo along the long call.
source: The density probability function of orangutan full pulses showed one peak (rk = 0.493) in close vicinity to a theoretically pure isochronic rhythm, that is, full pulses were regularly paced at a 1:1 ratio, following a constant tempo along the long call (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rhythm analysis data, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Pulse type, range of the curve (on-off-isochrony), and their interaction had a significant effect on the count of rk values (GLMM, full model vs null model: Chisq = 298.2876, df = 7, p<0.001).
source: Our model (GLMM, full model vs null model: Chisq = 298.2876, df = 7, p<0.001; see Supplementary file 1) showed that pulse type, range of the curve (on-off-isochrony), and their interaction had a significant effect on the count of rk values.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Full pulses' isochronous peak tested significant (t.ratio = −15.957, p<0.0001).
source: In particular, full pulses' isochronous peak tested significant (t.ratio = −15.957, p<0.0001), that is, the number of rk values falling inside the on-isochrony range was significantly higher than the number of rks falling inside the off-isochrony range (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Grumble sub-pulses showed significant peaks around pure isochrony (t.ratio = –5.940, p<0.0001; peak rk = 0.501).
source: Critically, three (of the four) orangutan sub-pulse element types – grumble sub-pulses, sub-pulse transitory elements, and bubble sub-pulses – also showed significant peaks (grumble sub-pulses: t.ratio = –5.940, p<0.0001; sub-pulse transitory elements: t.ratio = −4.048, p=0.0001; bubble sub-pulses: t.ratio = –10.640, p<0.0001) around pure isochrony (peak rk: grumble sub-pulses = 0.501; sub-pulse transitory elements = 0.495; bubble sub-pulses = 0.502; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Sub-pulse transitory elements showed significant peaks around pure isochrony (t.ratio = −4.048, p=0.0001; peak rk = 0.495).
source: Critically, three (of the four) orangutan sub-pulse element types – grumble sub-pulses, sub-pulse transitory elements, and bubble sub-pulses – also showed significant peaks (grumble sub-pulses: t.ratio = –5.940, p<0.0001; sub-pulse transitory elements: t.ratio = −4.048, p=0.0001; bubble sub-pulses: t.ratio = –10.640, p<0.0001) around pure isochrony (peak rk: grumble sub-pulses = 0.501; sub-pulse transitory elements = 0.495; bubble sub-pulses = 0.502; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Bubble sub-pulses showed significant peaks around pure isochrony (t.ratio = –10.640, p<0.0001; peak rk = 0.502).
source: Critically, three (of the four) orangutan sub-pulse element types – grumble sub-pulses, sub-pulse transitory elements, and bubble sub-pulses – also showed significant peaks (grumble sub-pulses: t.ratio = –5.940, p<0.0001; sub-pulse transitory elements: t.ratio = −4.048, p=0.0001; bubble sub-pulses: t.ratio = –10.640, p<0.0001) around pure isochrony (peak rk: grumble sub-pulses = 0.501; sub-pulse transitory elements = 0.495; bubble sub-pulses = 0.502; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's analysis, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Sub-pulses were regularly paced within regularly paced full pulses, denoting isochrony within isochrony at different average tempi.
source: That is, sub-pulses were regularly paced within regularly paced full pulses, denoting isochrony within isochrony (Figure 1C) at different average tempi [mean tk (sd): full pulses = 1.696 (0.508); grumble sub-pulses = 0.118 (0.111); sub-pulse transitory elements = 0.239 (0.468); bubble sub-pulses = 0.186 (0.292); Figure 1B].
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rhythm analysis data, illustrated in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Sub-pulses' tk was equivalent to 0.046 of their comprising full pulses, putting sub-pulses at an approximate ratio of 1:22 relative to that of full pulses.
source: Overall, sub-pulses' tk was equivalent to 0.046 of their comprising full pulses (Figure 1D), which puts sub-pulses at an approximate ratio of 1:22 relative to that of full pulses, the smallest categorical temporal rhythmic interval registered thus far in a vertebrate (De Gregorio et al., 2021; Roeske et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The 1:22 ratio between sub-pulses and full pulses represents the smallest categorical temporal rhythmic interval registered thus far in a vertebrate.
source: Overall, sub-pulses' tk was equivalent to 0.046 of their comprising full pulses (Figure 1D), which puts sub-pulses at an approximate ratio of 1:22 relative to that of full pulses, the smallest categorical temporal rhythmic interval registered thus far in a vertebrate (De Gregorio et al., 2021; Roeske et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparative claim based on the study's findings and citations to previous work.

claim: Permuted discriminant function analyses confirmed that grumble, transitory elements, and bubble sub-pulses represented acoustically distinct sub-pulse categories, with 62.7% of correctly classified selected cases, significantly higher than expected (p=0.001).
source: Permuted discriminant function analyses (Mundry and Sommer, 2007) (crossed, in order to control for individual variation) in R (R Development Core Team, 2013) based on seven acoustic measures extracted from grumble, transitory elements, and bubble sub-pulses confirmed that these represented indeed acoustically distinct sub-pulse categories, where the percentage of correctly classified selected cases (62.7%) was significantly higher (p=0.001) than expected (37%).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's acoustic analysis.

claim: Wild orangutan long calls exhibit two discernible structural strata – the full- and sub-pulse level.
source: Notably, we found that wild orangutan long calls exhibit two discernible structural strata – the full- and sub-pulse level – and three non-exclusive nested motifs in the form of [isochronyA [isochronya,b,c]](Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the study's analysis, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Wild orangutan long calls exhibit three non-exclusive nested motifs in the form of [isochronyA [isochronya,b,c]].
source: Notably, we found that wild orangutan long calls exhibit two discernible structural strata – the full- and sub-pulse level – and three non-exclusive nested motifs in the form of [isochronyA [isochronya,b,c]](Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary finding from the study's analysis, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The recursive vocal motifs in orangutan long calls are fundamentally distinct from simple repetition of calls or call isochrony.
source: This is fundamentally distinct from a simple repetition of calls or call isochrony – when a call repeats linearly at a constant interval – which are common features in some animal sound communication systems (De Gregorio et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a comparative claim distinguishing the study's findings from simpler vocal patterns, supported by citation.

claim: Simple repetition of calls or call isochrony are common features in some animal sound communication systems.
source: This is fundamentally distinct from a simple repetition of calls or call isochrony – when a call repeats linearly at a constant interval – which are common features in some animal sound communication systems (De Gregorio et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a claim about animal communication systems, supported by citation.

claim: The orangutans' production of recursive vocal motifs in the wild, without training, is especially compelling in the context of lab-based work showing that nonhuman animals can learn recursion with training.
source: The orangutans' production of recursive vocal motifs in the wild, and therefore, without training, is especially compelling in the context of the lab-based work that shows that nonhuman animals can learn recursion with training (Ferrigno et al., 2020; Gentner et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the findings in relation to previous laboratory studies, supported by citations.

claim: Some aspects of orangutan vocal combinatoric structures could be potentially learned.
source: Some aspects of these vocal combinatoric structures could be potentially learned as well (Lameira et al., 2022; Lameira et al., 2016; Lameira et al., 2015; Lameira and Shumaker, 2019b; Wich et al., 2012), but this study is agnostic on this matter because its design does not allow to single out learning effects.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about learning, supported by citations, with acknowledgment of the study's limitations.

claim: The study's design does not allow to single out learning effects in orangutan vocal combinatorics.
source: Some aspects of these vocal combinatoric structures could be potentially learned as well (Lameira et al., 2022; Lameira et al., 2016; Lameira et al., 2015; Lameira and Shumaker, 2019b; Wich et al., 2012), but this study is agnostic on this matter because its design does not allow to single out learning effects.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study's methodology.

claim: Temporal recursion occurs spontaneously in the wild in great ape vocal communication.
source: Nonetheless, results show that temporal recursion occurs spontaneously in the wild in great ape vocal communication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Humans perceive an acoustic pulse as a continuous pitch, instead of a rhythm, at rates higher than 30 Hz.
source: Humans perceive an acoustic pulse as a continuous pitch, instead of a rhythm, at rates higher than 30 Hz (i.e., 30 beats per second).
evidence: This is a claim about human auditory perception, drawing from established knowledge in psychoacoustics.

claim: Human and nonhuman great apes have similar auditory capacities.
source: Human and nonhuman great apes have similar auditory capacities (Quam et al., 2015), and there are limited skeletal differences in inner ear anatomy to suggest significantly distinct sensitivity, resolution, or activation thresholds in the time domain (Quam et al., 2015; Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Stoessel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative anatomical studies.

claim: There are limited skeletal differences in inner ear anatomy between humans and great apes to suggest significantly distinct sensitivity, resolution, or activation thresholds in the time domain.
source: Human and nonhuman great apes have similar auditory capacities (Quam et al., 2015), and there are limited skeletal differences in inner ear anatomy to suggest significantly distinct sensitivity, resolution, or activation thresholds in the time domain (Quam et al., 2015; Spoor and Zonneveld, 1998; Stoessel et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative anatomical studies.

claim: Long call sub-pulses exhibited average rhythms at ~9.263 (sd: 3.994) Hz.
source: Long call sub-pulses exhibited average rhythms at ~9.263 (sd: 3.994) Hz [i.e., tk = 0.184 (0.303) s].
evidence: This is a finding from the study's rhythm analysis.

claim: Orangutans (and other great apes), like humans, perceive sub-pulse rhythmic motifs at ~9.263 Hz as a train of signals, instead of one uninterrupted signal.
source: Therefore, ear anatomy offers confidence that orangutans (and other great apes), like humans, perceive sub-pulse rhythmic motifs at these rates as such, that is, a train of signals, instead of one uninterrupted signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative anatomy and the measured rhythm rates.

claim: The occurrence of three non-exclusive recursive patterns substantially decreases the probability that recursion was the by-product of anatomic constraints, such as vocal fold oscillation, breath length, heartbeat, and other physiological processes or movements.
source: The occurrence of three non-exclusive recursive patterns (i.e., three acoustically distinct sub-pulse calls occurring at three distinct tempi nested within the same pulse-level tempo) substantially decreases the probability that recursion was the by-product of anatomic constraints, such as vocal fold oscillation, breath length, heartbeat, and other physiological processes or movements (Pouw et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings about the multiple recursive patterns.

claim: In cases where nested patterns are by-products of physiological processes, sub-frequencies occur in the form of harmonics related to the reference frequency and to each other by small whole-numbered multiples.
source: Such processes can generate frequency patterns nested within others; however, in these cases, sub-frequencies occur in the form of harmonics related to the reference (dominant) frequency and to each other by small whole-numbered multiples.
evidence: This is a claim about the expected characteristics of physiologically-generated nested patterns, drawing from knowledge of acoustics and physiology.

claim: The three observed rhythmic arrangements at the sub-pulse level were not related to the pulse level by any small integer ratios (i.e., 1/22).
source: Yet, the three observed rhythmic arrangements at the sub-pulse level were not related to the pulse level by any small integer ratios (i.e., 1/22).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of rhythmic ratios.

claim: Recursive isochrony is not the absolute result of raw mechanics but is instead likely generated or tampered with by, at least, one temporally recursive neuro-motor procedure.
source: Together, our findings suggest that recursive isochrony is not the absolute result of raw mechanics but is instead likely generated or tampered with by, at least, one temporally recursive neuro-motor procedure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study's findings about the non-harmonic ratios and multiple patterns.

claim: To generate the observed vocal motifs linearly, three independent neuro-computational procedures would need to run in parallel.
source: To generate the observed vocal motifs linearly, three independent neuro-computational procedures would need to run in parallel.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be required for a linear algorithm to produce the observed patterns.

claim: If three independent linear procedures generated the vocal motifs, one would predict some degree of interference between the three linear procedures at the pulse level, manifested in some form of deviation around the isochrony peak.
source: If theoretically possible at all, one would predict some degree of interference between the three linear procedures at the pulse level, manifested in some form of deviation around the isochrony peak. However, this was not observed; distribution of data points on and off isochrony was equivalent between pulses and sub-pulses.
evidence: This is a logical prediction about expected interference, followed by a statement that this was not observed in the data.

claim: Distribution of data points on and off isochrony was equivalent between pulses and sub-pulses.
source: If theoretically possible at all, one would predict some degree of interference between the three linear procedures at the pulse level, manifested in some form of deviation around the isochrony peak. However, this was not observed; distribution of data points on and off isochrony was equivalent between pulses and sub-pulses.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Recursive self-embedded vocal motifs in orangutans indicate that vocal recursion among hominids is not exclusive to human vocal combinatorics, at least in the form of temporally embedded regular rhythms.
source: Recursive self-embedded vocal motifs in orangutans indicate that vocal recursion among hominids is not exclusive to human vocal combinatorics, at least in the form of temporally embedded regular rhythms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Orangutan recursive motifs do not exhibit all other properties that recursion exhibits in modern language-able humans.
source: This is not to suggest that orangutan recursive motifs exhibit all other properties that recursion exhibits in modern language-able humans, or that the two are the same, or equivalent.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the comparison between orangutan and human recursion.

claim: Expecting equivalence between orangutan recursive motifs and language recursion is unwarranted as it would imply that no evolution would have occurred in over 10 million years since the split between the orangutan and human lineages.
source: Expecting equivalence with language is, however, unwarranted as it would imply that no evolution would have occurred in over 10 million years since the split between the orangutan and human lineages.
evidence: This is a logical argument about evolutionary expectations.

claim: Differences between the study's findings and recursion in today's syntax, phonology, or music do not logically reject the possibility that recursive isochrony represents an ancient, and perhaps ancestral, state for the evolution of vocal recursion within the hominid family.
source: Any differences between our findings and recursion in today's syntax, phonology, or music do not logically reject the possibility that recursive isochrony represents an ancient, and perhaps ancestral, state for the evolution of vocal recursion within the hominid family.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the evolutionary interpretation of the findings.

claim: Recursion and fractal phenomena are prevalent across the universe.
source: Recursion and fractal phenomena are prevalent across the universe. Celestial and planetary movement, the splitting of tree branches, river deltas and arteries, and the morphology of bacteria colonies.
evidence: This is a claim about the ubiquity of recursive patterns in nature, drawing from general scientific knowledge.

claim: Patterns within self-similar patterns are the norm, not the exception in nature.
source: Patterns within self-similar patterns are the norm, not the exception.
evidence: This is a generalization about natural patterns, drawing from scientific knowledge.

claim: The discovery of recursive vocal patterns organized along two hierarchical temporal levels in a hominid besides humans suggests that 'sequences within sequences' may have been present in ancestral hominids.
source: The discovery of recursive vocal patterns organized along two hierarchical temporal levels in a hominid besides humans suggests that 'sequences within sequences' may have been present in ancestral hominids, and hence, that second-order sequences may have predated the emergence of language in the human lineage.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Second-order sequences may have predated the emergence of language in the human lineage.
source: The discovery of recursive vocal patterns organized along two hierarchical temporal levels in a hominid besides humans suggests that 'sequences within sequences' may have been present in ancestral hominids, and hence, that second-order sequences may have predated the emergence of language in the human lineage.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The possibility of self-embedded isochrony, or non-exclusive self-embedded patterns occurring within the same signal sequence, has on no account been formulated or conjectured as a possible state of recursive signaling.
source: Yet, the possibility of self-embedded isochrony, or non-exclusive self-embedded patterns occurring within the same signal sequence, has on no account been formulated or conjectured as a possible state of recursive signaling, be it in vertebrates, mammals, primates, or otherwise, extant or extinct.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings in relation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Controversy about recursion may have been underscored by data-poor circumstances on vocal combinatorics in wild great apes.
source: This suggests that controversy may have been underscored by data-poor circumstances on vocal combinatorics in wild great apes, which only now start gathering comprehensive research effort (Bortolato et al., 2023a; Bortolato et al., 2023b; Girard-Buttoz et al., 2022; but see Lameira et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is an inference about the reasons for previous controversy, supported by citations.

claim: Recursive vocal patterning in a wild great ape in the absence of syntax, semantics, phonology, or music opens a new charter for possible incipient and transitional states of recursion among hominids.
source: Recursive vocal patterning in a wild great ape in the absence of syntax, semantics, phonology, or music opens a new charter for possible incipient and transitional states of recursion among hominids.
evidence: This is a claim about the implications of the findings for understanding evolutionary transitions.

claim: Given the dearth of data on primate vocal combinatorics, it may be too hasty to discuss whether combinatorial capacities in primates or birds are equivalent to those engaged in syntax or phonology.
source: Given the dearth of such data, findings imply that it may be too hasty to discuss whether combinatorial capacities in primates or birds are equivalent to those engaged in syntax (Engesser et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2020) or phonology (Bowling and Fitch, 2015; Rawski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a cautionary inference about the state of the field, supported by citations.

claim: Classifications of animal vocal combinatorics as syntax-like or phonology-like may be based on untested assumptions that may not have applied to proto-recursive ancestors.
source: Such classifications may be putting the proverbial cart before the horse; they are based on untested assumptions that may not have applied to proto-recursive ancestors (Kershenbaum et al., 2014; Miyagawa, 2021), for example, that syntax and phonology evolved as separate 'modules', that one attained modern form before the other, or that they evolved in hominids regardless of whether consonant-like and vowel-like calls were present or not.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous approaches, supported by citations.

claim: Isochrony universally governs music.
source: Third, given that isochrony universally governs music and that recursion is a feature of music, findings could suggest a possible evolutionary link between great ape loud calls and vocal music.
evidence: This is a claim about music, drawing from musicological knowledge.

claim: Recursion is a feature of music.
source: Third, given that isochrony universally governs music and that recursion is a feature of music, findings could suggest a possible evolutionary link between great ape loud calls and vocal music.
evidence: This is a claim about music, drawing from musicological knowledge.

claim: Findings could suggest a possible evolutionary link between great ape loud calls and vocal music.
source: Third, given that isochrony universally governs music and that recursion is a feature of music, findings could suggest a possible evolutionary link between great ape loud calls and vocal music.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation of the findings.

claim: Loud calling is an archetypal trait in primates.
source: Loud calling is an archetypal trait in primates (Wich and Nunn, 2002) and among ancient hominids it could have preceded, and subsequently transmuted, into modern recursive vocal structures in humans, as found today in the form of song and chants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on primate loud calls.

claim: Among ancient hominids, loud calling could have preceded, and subsequently transmuted, into modern recursive vocal structures in humans, as found today in the form of song and chants.
source: Loud calling is an archetypal trait in primates (Wich and Nunn, 2002) and among ancient hominids it could have preceded, and subsequently transmuted, into modern recursive vocal structures in humans, as found today in the form of song and chants.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary scenario based on the findings.

claim: There are remarkably few confirmed cases of vocal isochrony in great apes.
source: Besides our analyses, there are remarkably few confirmed cases of vocal isochrony in great apes (but see Raimondi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a claim about the state of knowledge in the field, with a citation to one exception.

claim: Rhythmically measured behaviors in great apes have been implicated in the evolution of percussion and musical expression.
source: The behaviors that have been rhythmically measured with accuracy have been implicated in the evolution of percussion (Fuhrmann et al., 2015) and musical expression (Dufour et al., 2015; Hattori and Tomonaga, 2020), such as social entrainment in chimpanzees in connection with the origin of dance (Lameira et al., 2019a) (a capacity once also assumed to be neurologically impossible in great apes; Fitch, 2017; Patel, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on great ape rhythmic behaviors.

claim: Social entrainment in chimpanzees has been connected with the origin of dance.
source: The behaviors that have been rhythmically measured with accuracy have been implicated in the evolution of percussion (Fuhrmann et al., 2015) and musical expression (Dufour et al., 2015; Hattori and Tomonaga, 2020), such as social entrainment in chimpanzees in connection with the origin of dance (Lameira et al., 2019a) (a capacity once also assumed to be neurologically impossible in great apes; Fitch, 2017; Patel, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on chimpanzee social entrainment.

claim: The capacity for rhythmic entrainment was once assumed to be neurologically impossible in great apes.
source: The behaviors that have been rhythmically measured with accuracy have been implicated in the evolution of percussion (Fuhrmann et al., 2015) and musical expression (Dufour et al., 2015; Hattori and Tomonaga, 2020), such as social entrainment in chimpanzees in connection with the origin of dance (Lameira et al., 2019a) (a capacity once also assumed to be neurologically impossible in great apes; Fitch, 2017; Patel, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Recursive vocal combinatorics may have been first and foremost a feature of proto-musical expression in human ancestors, later recruited and 're-engineered' for the generation of linguistic combinatorics.
source: This opens the intriguing, tentative possibility that recursive vocal combinatorics were first and foremost a feature of proto-musical expression in human ancestors, later recruited and 're-engineered' for the generation of linguistic combinatorics.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: The presence of temporally recursive vocal motifs in a wild great ape revolutionizes how we can approach the evolution of recursion along the human lineage beyond all-or-nothing accounts.
source: The presence of temporally recursive vocal motifs in a wild great ape revolutionizes how we can approach the evolution of recursion along the human lineage beyond all-or-nothing accounts.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the findings for the field.

claim: Future studies on primate vocal combinatorics, particularly undertaking a structural approach and in the wild, offer promising new paths to empirically assess possible precursors and proto-states for the evolution of recursion within the hominid family.
source: Future studies on primate vocal combinatorics, particularly undertaking a structural approach and in the wild, offer promising new paths to empirically assess possible precursors and proto-states for the evolution of recursion within the hominid family, also adding temporal recursion as a new layer of analysis.
evidence: This is a claim about the implications of the findings for future research directions.

claim: The study was conducted at the Tuanan Research Station, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia.
source: We conducted our research at the Tuanan Research Station (2°09′S; 114°26′E), Central Kalimantan, Indonesia.
evidence: This describes the location of the study.

claim: Long calls were opportunistically recorded from identified flanged males (P. pygmaeus wurmbii) using specific recording equipment.
source: Long calls were opportunistically recorded from identified flanged males (P. pygmaeus wurmbii) using a Marantz Analogue Recorder PMD222 in combination with a Sennheiser Microphone ME 64 or a Sony Digital Recorder TCD-D100 in combination with a Sony Microphone ECM-M907.
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology.

claim: Audio recordings were transferred to a computer with a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz.
source: Audio recordings were transferred to a computer with a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claim: Seven acoustic measures were extracted directly from the spectrogram window using Raven interactive sound analysis software.
source: Seven acoustic measures were extracted directly from the spectrogram window (window type: Hann; 3 dB filter bandwidth: 124 Hz; grid frequency resolution: 2.69 Hz; grid time resolution: 256 samples) by manually drawing a selection encompassing the complete long call (sub)pulse from onset to offset using Raven interactive sound analysis software (version 1.5, Cornell Lab of Ornithology).
evidence: This describes the acoustic analysis methodology.

claim: Duration and peak frequency have been shown to be resilient across recording settings and adequately represent variation in the time and frequency axes.
source: Of these parameters, duration and peak frequency in particular have been shown to be resilient across recording settings (Lameira et al., 2013b) and adequately represent variation in the time and frequency axes (Lameira et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methodological work.
